column4: Fine standing horses are displayed to Solomon at evening, supplying the horse scene in which the next ayah's exact “love of good” wording occurs.
Solomon says that he loved the love of good while responding to the horses; حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ brings the runners and the exact love-of-good expression of 100:8 together outside surah 100.
The love of desires is adorned through gold, silver, and marked horses among other possessions, directly joining the ح ب ب family, prized wealth, and horses in one ayah.
Stones are described as bursting or splitting so that water emerges from them; the same hard object releases the opposite element from the section's spark-producing stone.
God erases the sign of night and makes the sign of day visible so people can seek bounty and reckon time, giving durable daylight the usefulness the section's instant sparks lack.
Night is a covering, sleep a rest, and day a rising again; the replacement of darkness by day becomes an image of resurrection, joining both major claims developed around the spark.
The voice at the fire tells Moses to remove his sandals because he is in the sacred valley Tuwa, identifying the fire-site as holy rather than merely a place to collect an ember.
God's call to Moses from the right side of the Mount and drawing him near recount the same revelatory encounter as the distant-fire narratives without repeating the fire detail.
The Lord calls Moses in the sacred valley Tuwa, another direct formulation of the encounter reached by following the fire in 20:10–13.
The addressee is reminded that he was not beside the Mount when God called; this retrospective reference confirms the fire journey as a revelatory scene transmitted as mercy.
God's call commissioning Moses to go to the wrongdoing people states the mission that comes out of the revelatory encounter first approached as a useful fire.
A clear flaming projectile pursues anyone who steals a hearing; the airborne شِهَاب repeats the useful firebrand word of 27:7 in a hostile celestial function.
A listener now finds a flaming projectile lying in wait, another concrete airborne شِهَاب set against Moses's portable ember and the horses' harmless sparks.
Seeking refuge in the Lord of daybreak presents dawn as an opening cut through darkness, a nonlexical parallel to the section's morning that replaces the spark-lit night.
The blast seizes the people of Lot in the morning, repeating the ص ب ح boundary as the arrival of destruction rather than benign illumination.
The warned are told how evil their morning will be when punishment descends, making صباح carry the opposite valence from the section's lasting morning light.
After thinking and looking, the man turns away in arrogance; this ayah marks the decisive misuse of the deliberation whose false verdict follows.
Saqar neither leaves nor spares, setting total consumption against the source's account of fire leaving ash behind.
Skins consumed by fire are replaced so that punishment is tasted anew, a concrete Quranic instance of fire transforming the surface it touches.
Hell is set ablaze at the final upheaval, placing ignition itself inside the resurrection horizon that the section reaches through ordinary kindling.
The trench contains a fire full of fuel, foregrounding the prepared combustible material required for a spark to become sustained flame.
A human construction founded at a crumbling brink collapses with its builder into Hellfire, giving the section's successful-versus-wasted undertaking question a material and fiery form.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living and revives earth after death; this states the reversal made tangible when fire issues from a green tree.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the guided people of understanding, a positive counterpart to striking the source dictionary's “flint of misguidance.”
People destined for Hell have hearts with which they do not understand, repeating the precise link between failed human reason and fire stated in 67:10.
“We created you; why do you not affirm?” introduces the divine agency that the following crop, water, and fire questions unfold against resurrection denial.
After the imagined crop is crushed, people recognize themselves as burdened by loss, registering the failure of what had seemed a successful human undertaking.
The further admission that they are deprived makes explicit that useful provision was never secured by human effort alone.
Lightning from the clouds nearly snatches sight, another Quranic flash whose intense but momentary light differs from the stable light of morning and lamp.
Iron is sent down with great strength and benefits for people; the metal used as the section's striking tool is here explicitly measured by durable human benefit.
A person's wealth will not benefit him when he falls, restating the image's question of whether prized gain becomes any lasting or useful result.
The warning of a blazing fire supplies the fiery outcome of the nearby miser's self-sufficiency and wealth that cannot benefit him.
